ideas: thinks it is just lack of exercise and poor stamina

clinical_knowledge.topic: Stable Angina (Coronary Artery Disease) evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Stable Angina (Coronary Artery Disease) is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Standard management emphasizes confirming the diagnosis with objective ischaemia testing, then initiating evidence-based anti-anginal and secondary-prevention therapy for Stable Angina Pectoris (Coronary Artery Disease), adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: chest discomfort and shortness of breath when walking that resolves with rest

Key HPI features: 52M business traveler reports 1 month of pressure-like chest tightness and mild shortness of breath whenever he walks fast at airports or walks uphill. The feeling resolves within 5 minutes of resting. Denies rest pain.

Objective/Exam findings: Vitals typically normal at rest. Cardiac auscultation usually normal without murmurs or gallops. 12-lead resting ECG often normal or shows minor non-specific ST/T changes (a normal resting ECG does not exclude stable angina). Outpatient functional ischaemia testing (exercise stress test, stress echocardiogram, or CT coronary angiography) to confirm the diagnosis.
Current medications: Lisinopril 10mg daily, Atorvastatin 20mg daily
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Stable Angina (Coronary Artery Disease).
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to GERD without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Symptoms at rest or with steadily less effort than before.
management_principles: Confirm the diagnosis with outpatient exercise stress test or coronary CTA
Optimize anti-anginal therapy and address cardiovascular risk factors; use antiplatelet and statin therapy when coronary artery disease is confirmed or otherwise indicated
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

The feeling resolves within 5 minutes of resting. Denies rest pain.
reference_soap.objective: Vitals typically normal at rest. Outpatient functional ischaemia testing (exercise stress test, stress echocardiogram, or CT coronary angiography) to confirm the diagnosis.
reference_soap.assessment: Stable Angina Pectoris (Coronary Artery Disease) — exertional chest tightness and dyspnoea reproducible at a fixed workload and relieved by rest, in a patient with hypertension, hyperlipidaemia, and active smoking. DDx: GERD, musculoskeletal chest pain, anaemia.
reference_soap.plan: Confirm the diagnosis with outpatient exercise stress test or coronary CTA. Optimize anti-anginal therapy and address cardiovascular risk factors; use antiplatelet and statin therapy when coronary artery disease is confirmed or otherwise indicated. Refer to specialty team and provide comprehensive patient counseling, including smoking cessation.

Select appropriate laboratory and imaging studies for cardiovascular risk stratification, including exercise stress testing and coronary CT angiography
Implement evidence-based acute and long-term management strategies for Stable Angina Pectoris (Coronary Artery Disease).

teaching.one_liner: Narrowed coronary arteries that keep up at rest but not on effort — discomfort appears at a reproducible workload.
red_flags: Symptoms at rest or with steadily less effort than before

must_ask.say: Does it come on when you walk uphill or climb stairs, and settle when you rest?
How would you describe it — sharp, crushing, burning, tight?

must_ask.objective: Site and radiation of the pain
must_ask.say: Where exactly is the pain, and does it move anywhere else?
Do you get short of breath at the same point as the chest discomfort?
Do you have high blood pressure, diabetes, or high cholesterol, and do you smoke?

must_ask.objective: Family history of early heart disease
must_ask.say: Has anyone in your family had a heart attack, especially young?

history.answer: Whenever I walk fast through airports or walk uphill, my chest feels tight and I get short of breath.
This started about a month ago, and it happens gradually whenever I exert myself.
It feels like a heavy pressure right across the center of my chest, behind my breastbone. I cannot pinpoint it with one finger.
Sometimes the tightness spreads slightly into my left shoulder and inner left arm, but not to my jaw or back.
Each spell lasts about three to five minutes and goes away completely once I stop and sit down.
When it happens, it feels like a 5 out of 10 in tightness, but right now I have no pain at all.
Walking fast or climbing stairs definitely brings it on, and resting makes it go away completely. I have never had it while resting or sleeping.
No, taking a deep breath or coughing does not change the feeling at all.
Changing my position does not help or hurt, and pressing on my chest does not hurt either.
No, it has nothing to do with meals, lying down flat, or swallowing, and I do not have acid reflux or heartburn.
history.topic: Relationship to meals and acid reflux

history.answer: I feel mildly short of breath when the chest tightness comes on, but I have not had cold sweats, nausea, vomiting, dizziness, or fainting.
history.topic: Associated shortness of breath and sweating

history.answer: No, I have had no fever, chills, cough, or phlegm.
No, I have been feeling completely well otherwise and have not had a cold or flu recently.
I travel by plane often for work, but I have not had any leg swelling, calf pain, or recent surgeries.
No, my skin is clear and there are no rashes or blisters on my chest.
No, I do not have panic attacks, numbness in my hands, or sudden terror, just concern about my heart when I exert myself.
No, I have never had an injury to my chest or done any heavy lifting or repetitive chest workouts.
I have never had chest tightness like this before, and I have never had a heart stent or an angiogram.
history.topic: Previous chest pain and heart procedures

history.answer: I initially thought it was just poor stamina and lack of exercise, but I am worried one of my heart arteries might be blocked.
I am hoping to get my heart properly checked out today, perhaps with a stress test.
I was diagnosed with high blood pressure and high cholesterol about five years ago. I do not have diabetes.
I had an appendectomy when I was in college, but no other surgeries or hospitalizations.
I take Lisinopril 10 milligrams and Atorvastatin 20 milligrams once every morning. I do not take any over-the-counter supplements or aspirin.
I do not have any known allergies to medications.
I have smoked about half a pack of cigarettes a day for the past twenty-five years.
I drink one or two glasses of beer once or twice a week when dining with clients.
I work as a regional sales manager, which involves frequent domestic flights. I live with my wife and teenage son.
My father had a heart attack in his late fifties, but my mother is alive and well.

exam.finding: Blood pressure 128/82 mmHg, heart rate 72 beats per minute, respiratory rate 14 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 98% on room air, body temperature 36.6°C.
Comfortable appearance at rest without distress, pallor, or diaphoresis.
Pink conjunctivae without pallor; anicteric sclerae.
Normal jugular venous pressure without venous distension.
No chest wall deformities, rash, or tenderness to palpation across the sternum and ribs.
Resonant percussion notes bilaterally throughout all lung fields.
Clear vesicular breath sounds bilaterally without wheezes or crackles.
Regular rate and rhythm with normal S1 and S2, without murmurs, gallops, or pericardial friction rubs.
Soft, non-tender abdomen without epigastric pain or organomegaly.
No pitting edema in either lower extremity.
Calves are symmetric, non-tender, and without swelling or warmth.
